## Setting

The [[black-scholes-merton-model|Black-Scholes PDE]] for a European call with
strike $K$ and maturity $T$ has value function $u(t,x)$, a function of time
$t$ and asset price $x$, solving the [[partial-differential-equations|PDE]]

$$
\begin{cases}
\partial_t u + rx\,\partial_x u + \dfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2x^2\,\partial_{xx}u
- ru = 0, \\[1ex]
u(T,x) = (x-K)_+ .
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
$$

Here $r$ is the risk-free rate and $\sigma$ the volatility. The **finite
difference (FD) method** discretises the continuous domain of $(t,x)$ into a
mesh with steps $(\Delta t,\Delta x)$ and replaces each derivative by a
difference quotient obtained from a Taylor expansion around the mesh point.

## Difference Quotients

For example, the time derivative is the limit

$$
\partial_t u = \lim_{\delta t\to 0}\frac{u(t+\delta t,x)-u(t,x)}{\delta t}
\approx \frac{u(t+\Delta t,x)-u(t,x)}{\Delta t} + O(\Delta t),
$$

for small $\Delta t$. This is a **forward difference**. There are three
first-order approximations.

:::{.definition data-title="Forward, Backward and Central Differences"}

1. **Forward difference:**
   $$
   \partial_t u \approx \frac{u(t+\Delta t,x)-u(t,x)}{\Delta t},
   $$
2. **Backward difference:**
   $$
   \partial_t u \approx \frac{u(t,x)-u(t-\Delta t,x)}{\Delta t},
   $$
3. **Central difference:**
   $$
   \partial_t u \approx \frac{u(t+\Delta t,x)-u(t-\Delta t,x)}{2\Delta t}.
   $$

:::

The same formulas hold for $\partial_x u$ with $x$ in place of $t$. The
forward and backward differences have error $O(\Delta t)$, the central
difference $O(\Delta t^2)$.

For second derivatives, taking the forward difference of the backward
difference (or the reverse) gives the same quotient.

:::{.definition data-title="Symmetric Second Difference"}

$$
\partial_{xx}u \approx \frac{u(t,x+\Delta x)-2u(t,x)+u(t,x-\Delta x)}
{(\Delta x)^2},
$$

with error $O((\Delta x)^2)$, so accuracy improves faster under mesh
refinement than for the first-order quotients above.

:::

## The Mesh

Specify $x_{\min}$, $x_{\max}$, $t_{\min}$, $t_{\max}$, $\Delta x$ and
$\Delta t$. For the call (1) we take $x_{\min}=0$ and $t_{\min}=0$, since
price and time are non-negative, and $x_{\max}=N\Delta x$ large, $T=M\Delta t$.
Write

$$
u_n^m = u(m\Delta t,\,n\Delta x),\qquad n=0,\dots,N,\quad m=0,\dots,M.
$$

## Explicit Scheme

Use the forward difference in time $\partial_t u\approx(u_n^{m+1}-u_n^m)/\Delta t$,
and the central and symmetric differences in space,

$$
\partial_x u\approx\frac{u_{n+1}^{m+1}-u_{n-1}^{m+1}}{2\Delta x},\qquad
\partial_{xx}u\approx\frac{u_{n+1}^{m+1}-2u_n^{m+1}+u_{n-1}^{m+1}}{(\Delta x)^2},
$$

all evaluated at the *later* time level. Substituting into (1) with
$x=n\Delta x$ and solving for $u_n^m$ gives the backward recursion

$$
u_n^{m}=P_n^+u_{n+1}^{m+1}+P_n^0u_n^{m+1}+P_n^-u_{n-1}^{m+1},
$$

where

$$
P_n^{\pm}=\frac{\Delta t}{2}\left(\sigma^2n^2\pm rn\right),\qquad
P_n^0=1-\Delta t\left(\sigma^2n^2+r\right).
$$

The terminal condition is $u_n^M=(n\Delta x-K)_+$, with boundary values
$u_0^m=0$ and $u_N^m\approx N\Delta x-Ke^{-r(T-m\Delta t)}$. The recursion
looks like a trinomial tree run backwards in time. It is cheap, but only stable
if $\Delta t$ is small enough that $P_n^0\ge 0$, roughly
$\Delta t\le 1/(\sigma^2N^2+r)$.

## Implicit and Crank-Nicolson Schemes

The **implicit scheme** evaluates the spatial differences at the *earlier*
time level $m$. This gives, for each $m$, a tridiagonal linear system

$$
A\,u^{m}=u^{m+1},
$$

for the vector $u^m=(u_n^m)_n$, which is solved backwards in time. It is
unconditionally stable. The **Crank-Nicolson scheme** averages the explicit
and implicit spatial differences, which makes it second-order accurate in
time as well as in space (error $O(\Delta t^2+\Delta x^2)$) and also
unconditionally stable.

## American Options

The explicit scheme is consistent with early exercise, since it is a
[[binomial-model|tree-like]] procedure that moves backwards in time. As for
a tree, we force $V\ge G$ for the value function $V(t,s)$ and immediate
payoff $G(t,s)=(K-s)_+$ (an American put) by taking the maximum of the two at
every grid point,

$$
V_n^{m}\leftarrow \max\{V_n^{m},\,G_n^{m}\}.
$$

This gives the correct price because each $V_n^m$ is computed from the later
level $m+1$ and is never changed again. After solving, one exercises early
exactly where $V(t,s)=G(t,s)$, which gives the exercise boundary.

For the implicit scheme this pointwise maximum is **wrong**. The scheme
couples $V_{n-1}^m$, $V_n^m$ and $V_{n+1}^m$ in one linear equation, so
altering one grid point changes its neighbours and eventually every
$V_i^m$.

Instead one uses **projected SOR (PSOR)**, which solves the linear system
$AV^m=b$ by successive over-relaxation and projects each iterate onto
$V\ge G$:

$$
V_i^{m,(k+1)}=\max\left\{G_i^m,\;(1-w)V_i^{m,(k)}+\frac{w}{A_{ii}}\left(
b_i-\sum_{j<i}A_{ij}V_j^{m,(k+1)}-\sum_{j>i}A_{ij}V_j^{m,(k)}\right)\right\},
$$

where $k$ is the iteration index and $w\in(1,2)$ the relaxation parameter. The
iteration converges to the solution of the system restricted to
$\{V\ge G\}$. As before, the exercise boundary is where $V=G$.
